doc.title: Phil Flanigan interviewed by Monk Rowe, San Diego, California, February 15, 1998

title: Roy Eldridge, Jilly's and Frank Sinatra's crowd
summary: Eldridge embraced the band, who worked at Jilly's where Sinatra's friends hung out.

story.theme_name: Coming to New York: clubs, jams, and making it
story.community_name: Making it in New York: arrival, clubs and the scene

blocks.x: Thank you. Breaking into New York, well Roy Eldridge was the other guy besides who I mentioned already that really embraced Scott and us. Because by then we were a sort of band and worked together. We worked at Jilly’s, for Jilly Rizzo, you know Frank’s friend.

Oh you don’t know Jilly’s? The club in New York. It was big in — how shall I say it — the powerful Italian people would congregate there. And it was a hangout of Frank’s, Frank S. And those people loved to have a good time and back then throughout the ‘40s, ‘50s and ‘60s they hired good music a lot of them. They had good taste in music in my opinion. And we sort of fit into that crowd for a few minutes. That scene was sort of on the way down by the time we got there, ‘76, ‘77. But Jilly loved us and Frank came by a couple of times. It was gratifying to even get some attention from these people. And a lot of the people in New York would listen to these kind of people and if you were all right with them then you were okay, and then you might work at another place like Jimmy Weston’s, and then you might work at blah, blah, blah. Not that those kind of affiliations amounted to anything really, but they were tolerant of us and we were tolerant of them and we were all very happy with the arrangement. I see it as — we could use a little more of that these days, in the politically correct, over bureaucracized, over administered scene that we have.
